02

Find the Sun’s elevation

Rough Street View estimates are prefilled: Mast 1 ≈9 m, Mast 2 ≈10 m, each with a working ±3 m bound. Replace these when measured heights are available. A complete second reference checks the first.

Height is vertical from bare ground to the point casting the measured shadow. Shadow length runs from the mast base to that point’s shadow on the ground. Similar fittings do not establish equal installed heights.

Use the elevation above the horizon at the actual image acquisition date and time, not the Sun’s compass direction.

Measurement bounds optional

Enter ± bounds on the inputs. These produce a worst-case sensitivity range, not a confidence interval. Zero leaves that source of uncertainty unmodeled.

A separation bound can explore camera displacement, but it does not reconstruct the true glider position or its underlying terrain.

THE METHOD

One ray of sunlight, two terrain elevations.

1. Calibrate with a vertical mast

tan(α) = (hmast + zbase − zmast shadow) / L

The mast height and its horizontal shadow length determine the Sun’s elevation after correcting for the ground slope.

2. Apply the angle to the glider

H = D × tan(α) + zshadow − zbeneath

H is the vertical height of the selected glider point above the ground directly beneath it. The current terrain correction is approximately −21.4 m.

3. Check the image geometry

SWISSIMAGE is an aerial orthophoto mosaic projected onto terrain. An airborne object can appear displaced. Match corresponding glider and shadow points, verify source acquisition times, and assess camera displacement before reporting a final height.

Sources: SWISSIMAGE & acquisition dates · Orthophoto displacement, §1.7 · Swiss terrain API
